questions.question: Two number lines both run from 0 to 2. On Line A, each whole is cut into 3 equal parts, and a dot sits 5 parts to the right of 0. On Line B, each whole is cut into 4 equal parts, and a dot sits 6 parts to the right of 0. Which dot is farther to the right?
options: Line A's dot, because 5/3 = 20/12 and 6/4 = 18/12
Line B's dot, because fourths are bigger pieces than thirds
They land on the same spot, because each dot is 2 parts past the 1
Line B's dot, because 6 parts is more than 5 parts
questions.explain: Rename both with the common denominator 12: 5/3 = 20/12 and 6/4 = 18/12, so 5/3 is farther right. The trap is thinking a bigger denominator means bigger pieces — cutting a whole into 4 parts makes each part smaller than a third, and counting raw parts (6 beats 5) only works when the parts are the same size.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 3. Each whole is cut into 8 equal parts. A counter sits 11 parts to the right of 0. Does the counter land before, after, or exactly on the halfway mark between 1 and 2 (the point 1 1/2)?
options: After 1 1/2, because 11 parts is more than the 8 parts in one whole
Before 1 1/2, because the counter is at 1 3/8 and 3/8 is less than 4/8
After 1 1/2, because eighths are bigger pieces than halves, so 3/8 is more than 1/2
Exactly on 1 1/2, because 1 3/8 rounds up to 1 1/2
questions.explain: Eleven eighths is 1 3/8, and the benchmark 1 1/2 is 1 4/8, so the counter stops before it. The common trap is deciding 3/8 beats 1/2 because 8 is a bigger number — more equal parts means each part is smaller.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 3 and each whole is cut into 6 equal parts. Dot P sits 8 parts to the right of 0. Dot Q sits on the whole number 2. Dot R is at the labelled point 1 1/2. Reading the line from left to right, in what order do the dots appear?
options: Q, P, R, because the whole number 2 has no fraction part, so it is the smallest
R, P, Q, because sixths are bigger pieces than halves, so 1 2/6 is past 1 1/2
P, R, Q, because P is 8/6 = 1 2/6, then R is 1 1/2 = 1 3/6, then Q is 2
R, Q, P, because P sits at 8 parts and 8 is the biggest number in the question
questions.explain: Put everything in sixths: P is 1 2/6, R is 1 3/6, and Q is 2, so the order is P, R, Q. Two traps to dodge — a whole number is not automatically the smallest, and 1/6 is not bigger than 1/2 just because 6 is bigger than 2.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 3. Each whole is cut into 10 equal parts. Dot A sits 12 parts to the right of 0. Dot B is at the labelled point 1 1/5. Which statement about the two dots is true?
options: Dot A is farther right, because tenths are bigger pieces than fifths
Dot A is farther right, because 12 parts is more than one whole and one part
Dot B is farther right, because one fifth is a bigger piece than two tenths
They sit on exactly the same point, because 1 1/5 = 1 2/10 and dot A is at 1 2/10
questions.explain: Rename 1/5 in tenths: 1/5 = 2/10, so 1 1/5 is 1 2/10, which is exactly where 12 tenths lands — the dots match. Watch the trap of judging by denominator size; tenths are smaller pieces than fifths, but two of them equal one fifth.

questions.question: Which list puts 7/4, 1 5/8 and 2 in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Write them all in eighths: 7/4 = 1 6/8, the mixed number is 1 5/8, and 2 = 2 0/8, so the order is 1 5/8, then 7/4, then 2. The usual slip is calling 5/8 bigger than 6/8 because eighths sound like more pieces — with the same denominator, just compare the numerators.

questions.question: At the Kelowna skate park, Priya rolled 2 1/3 km and Owen rolled 9/4 km. Who travelled farther?
options: Owen, because 9/4 = 2 1/4 and quarters are bigger pieces than thirds
Priya, because 2 1/3 = 28/12 and 9/4 = 27/12
Owen, because 9 is a much bigger number than 2
They tied, because both distances are between 2 km and 3 km
questions.explain: Change 9/4 to 2 1/4, then use the common denominator 12: Priya is at 2 4/12 and Owen at 2 3/12, so Priya went farther. The traps are comparing a numerator (9) with a whole number (2), and assuming quarters beat thirds because 4 is bigger than 3.

questions.question: Marcus needs to decide whether 15/8 is less than, equal to, or greater than 2. Which method is both correct and quickest?
options: Round 15/8 up to 2, so the two numbers are equal
The denominator 8 is large, so 15/8 must be greater than 2
Write 2 as 16/8; since 15 is less than 16, 15/8 is less than 2
15 is greater than 2, so 15/8 is greater than 2
questions.explain: Turn the whole number into eighths (2 = 16/8) so both numbers share a denominator, then compare numerators: 15/8 is less than 2. Rounding first destroys the comparison, and a large denominator means small pieces, not a large number.

questions.question: Three water jugs at a Burnaby soccer practice hold 7/2 L, 3 3/8 L and 3 1/4 L. Which jug holds the most?
options: The 3 3/8 L jug, because eighths are bigger pieces than halves
They all hold the same, because each amount is between 3 L and 4 L
The 3 1/4 L jug, because 4 is the smallest denominator, so its pieces are the biggest
The 7/2 L jug, because 7/2 = 3 4/8, which beats 3 3/8 and 3 2/8
questions.explain: Write every amount in eighths: 7/2 = 3 4/8, next 3 3/8, and 3 1/4 = 3 2/8, so the 7/2 L jug wins. Bigger pieces alone do not decide the winner — you must count how many pieces there are, using one common denominator.

questions.question: Ravi is training on the Coquitlam trails. He ran 11/4 km on Monday and 2 5/8 km on Tuesday. His coach's rule is that a training run must be MORE than 2 3/4 km to count. On which day or days did Ravi meet the rule?
options: Neither day, because 11/4 is exactly 2 3/4 (not more), and 2 5/8 is less than 2 6/8
Tuesday only, because 5/8 is bigger than 3/4 since eighths beat fourths
Monday only, because 11/4 is an improper fraction, so it must be the bigger amount
Both days, because both runs are longer than 2 km
questions.explain: Change 11/4 to 2 3/4 — it equals the target, so it is not more than it — and rewrite 2 3/4 as 2 6/8 to see that Tuesday's 2 5/8 falls short. Being improper does not make a fraction large, and 5/8 is less than 3/4, not more, even though 8 is bigger than 4.

questions.question: In a Victoria craft class, five ribbons measure 3/2 m, 5/4 m, 2 m, 9/4 m and 1 m. What is the median (middle) length?
options: 5/4 m, because 5/4 is greater than 3/2 (fourths beat halves)
3/2 m, because in order the lengths are 1, 5/4, 3/2, 2, 9/4
2 m, because 2 sits in the middle of the list the way it is written
9/4 m, because the median is the longest ribbon
questions.explain: For a median you must order the values first: in quarters they are 4/4, 5/4, 6/4, 8/4, 9/4, so the middle one is 6/4 = 3/2 m. Never read the middle straight off the unsorted list, and remember 5/4 is smaller than 3/2 even though 4 is bigger than 2.

questions.question: Leah is placing numbers on a number line and says: 'The point 4 1/6 comes after 4 1/5, because sixths are bigger than fifths.' What is the best response to Leah?
options: Leah is right — 6 is bigger than 5, so 1/6 is the bigger piece
They land on the same point, because both are 4 wholes and one piece
Leah is wrong — cutting a whole into 6 parts makes smaller pieces, so 1/6 is less than 1/5 and 4 1/6 comes first
You cannot compare them at all until both are changed into improper fractions
questions.explain: The whole numbers match, so compare the fraction parts with a common denominator: 1/6 = 5/30 and 1/5 = 6/30, so 4 1/6 sits to the left of 4 1/5. The misconception is that a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction — more equal parts always means each part is smaller.

questions.question: Three cyclists ride the Galloping Goose trail: Mei rides 17/5 km, Jon rides 3 1/2 km and Sam rides 3 km. Whose distance is in the middle of the three?
options: Jon, because 1/2 is smaller than 2/5 since fifths beat halves, so 3 1/2 sits between 3 and 17/5
No one, because 17/5 is bigger than both — 17 is the largest number written
Sam, because 3 has no fraction part, so it sits between the other two
questions.explain: Change 17/5 to 3 2/5, then use the common denominator 10: Sam has 30/10, Mei 34/10 and Jon 35/10, so Mei is in the middle. Do not compare 17 with 3, and remember 2/5 is less than 1/2 even though 5 is bigger than 2.
